entries.author: Plato
entries.date_note: Classical Greek text; commonly dated to the 4th century BCE
supports: Aristophanes' myth of originally whole humans divided and seeking reunion
historical antecedent for later split-pair imagery

entries.author: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
entries.date_note: Ancient Upanishadic text; dating varies by scholarship
supports: a cosmogonic passage in which a primordial self divides into husband and wife
does_not_support: one unique romantic counterpart for every contemporary person
entries.translation_note: Online translation used as locator; critical editions/translations should be preferred in formal scholarship.

entries.author: H. P. Blavatsky
entries.passage: p. 170, 'Additional Facts and Explanations Concerning the Globes and the Monads'
supports: Theosophical use of Monad terminology within evolutionary/cosmological doctrine
does_not_support: automatic equivalence between Theosophical Monad and a romantic twin-flame pair

entries.author: Alice A. Bailey
entries.passage: Chapter II, Question 1: What is the soul?
supports: a distinct esoteric account of spirit, soul, personality and embodied form
does_not_support: automatic attribution of a canonical romantic twin-flame doctrine to Bailey

entries.author: The Summit Lighthouse / Elizabeth Clare Prophet tradition
supports: explicit modern distinction among twin flames, soul mates and karmic relationships
doctrine that twin flames were created together in a single fiery ovoid and differentiated into masculine/feminine polarity
does_not_support: astrological proof that any specific pair belongs to the category

entries.author: The Summit Lighthouse
supports: organizational definition of twin flame as masculine or feminine counterpart conceived from the same white-fire body
bibliographic pointers to 1978, 1985 and later Summit Lighthouse materials
does_not_support: historical priority over all earlier uses of twin-flame language

entries.author: Kennet Granholm
entries.work: The Sociology of Esotericism, in The Oxford Handbook of the Sociology of Religion
supports: academic contextualization of modern Western esotericism and New Age spirituality
